hello: A program is a recipe: a list of steps the computer follows in order, from top to bottom. In Blockly, each step is a block, and blocks that snap together run one after the other. Print is your window into the program: whatever value you give it appears in the output. The first print holds a fixed piece of text, Hello, world. The second print holds a question instead: a Noul block that asks Jev whether this text is a greeting. When the program runs, Jev reads the text and hands back true or false, and to the program that is just another value. Now your turn: print a greeting in another language, then print two Nouls about it, one asking whether it is a greeting, and one asking whether it is written in Spanish.
variables: Typing the same text three times invites mistakes. A variable gives a value a name, so you write it once and refer to it by name everywhere else. Set message to stores the text under the name message, and the round message block reads it back. The program prints the message, then asks a Noul probability about it: does the writer sound happy. The answer is a number between zero and one: zero point nine five is a confident yes, zero point zero five a confident no, and zero point five means Jev cannot tell. Because it is a number, you can store it, compare it, add it, and print it like any other value. Your turn: store a message in a variable, then print two probabilities about it, how likely the writer sounds happy, and how likely they sound worried.
if-else: So far every block ran, and programs get interesting when they choose. If, then, else looks at a condition, a value that is true or false, and runs only one of its two branches. The branch that does not run is simply skipped. Here the condition is a Noul asking whether the message is a question, and the if Noul block folds the question and the decision into one. Yes if at least zero point five is the threshold: yes wins when the probability of yes reaches that number. Raise the threshold when a wrong yes is costly, and lower it when a missed yes is costly. Your turn: decide whether a message is a complaint, print send to support when it is and send to marketing otherwise, and only call it a complaint when Jev is at least zero point seven sure.
numbers: Numbers are values you can calculate with and compare. The compare block takes two values and an operator, such as less than, equal, or at least, and produces true or false, which any if can use. A Score turns text into a number on a scale you define: here zero means rude, one means neutral, and two means polite. Jev returns the expected position on that scale, so one point six means between neutral and polite, closer to polite. Because the result is a number, the threshold lives in your code: at least one point five means reply warmly, anything less means reply carefully. Change the comparison and the program behaves differently without asking Jev anything new. Your turn: score a message's urgency on three levels, no rush, soon, right now, print the score, then print handle today when it is above one, and can wait otherwise.
switch: Two branches are often not enough. A switch lists several cases and runs exactly one of them, the one that matches, and it reads better than a pile of nested ifs. Switch Choice asks Jev to pick one of your cases: which team should handle this ticket, billing, technical, or sales. Each case has a label, which becomes the answer, and a description that tells Jev what the label covers, and good descriptions matter more than clever labels. Jev also reports confidence, how concentrated its pick was. The otherwise branch runs when confidence is below the limit you set, so unclear tickets go to a person instead of a wrong team. Your turn: build a language router that replies in Spanish, English, or French depending on the message, and otherwise asks which language this is.
lists-loops: A list holds several values in order: three messages, ten scores, a hundred names. You build one with create list with, and it behaves as a single value you can store and pass around. A loop repeats blocks: for each item in list runs its body once per element, and each time puts the current element into the loop variable. Three messages, three runs, no copy and paste. Put a Jev block inside the loop and it runs once per item: here a Choice names the language of each message, English, Spanish, or French. That is how a judgment about one message becomes a judgment about every message. Your turn: for each of three messages, print the message, an arrow, and a Noul saying whether it is a question.
counting: A counter is a variable that starts at zero and grows inside a loop. Change positive by one adds one to it, and when the loop ends, the counter holds a total you could not know before running. Notice the shape: set to zero before the loop, change inside the loop, print after. Almost every summary in programming, totals, averages, maxima, follows this shape. Inside the loop an if guards the increment: only reviews Jev judges positive count, so the judgment is per item and the arithmetic is yours. Three small judgments become one useful number: positive reviews, two of three. Your turn: count how many of three messages are questions, and print questions, N of three.
logic: And, or, and not combine truth values. A and B is true only when both are, A or B when at least one is, and not A flips it. With these three you can write any rule. A rule with several parts is clearer when each part is its own judgment: is it urgent, and is the writer angry, are two simple Nouls. The rule that combines them is visible in the blocks, not hidden in a long question. Keeping judgments separate also makes them reusable: the same is angry Noul can feed several different rules. Your turn: print priority when a message is urgent or angry, but only if it is not spam, and normal otherwise, using three separate Nouls.
functions: When the same blocks are needed in two places, wrap them in a function: a named group of blocks. Calling the function by name runs the group, and if you change the group once, every call changes. A function can take inputs, called parameters: mood of takes text, and each call passes a different message. Inside the function, the name text refers to whatever was passed in. A function can return a value, so a call can sit inside a join or a print like any other value. Here the function wraps one Choice, joyful, frustrated, or calm, and calling it twice reuses the same judgment on two messages without copying blocks. Your turn: define a function is urgent with one parameter, text, that returns a Noul, then call it on two different messages and print both results with a label.
assistant: Real programs are the nine ideas so far, combined. Read this one from the top: a counter, a list, a loop, a function call, a variable, a Score, a print, an if with a comparison, and a final print. Notice the division of labour. Jev answers narrow questions: which category, how urgent. Your blocks hold the policy: what counts as urgent, what to print, what to count. Change the policy and nothing about the questions changes. This is the habit to keep: ask the model for a judgment, keep the rules in code, and let the output show both, so you can see why the program did what it did. Your turn: add a second counter, priority, that grows only when the category is billing and the urgency is above one point five, and print both totals at the end.
